content.p: For a generation of Sydney readers, Roger Rogerson was both the best and the worst of what a New South Wales detective could be. He won his force's top annual award in 1980. Within six years he had been dismissed, and over the following decades he was jailed twice for offences connected with his conduct, once for perverting the course of justice and once for lying to an anti-corruption body. In 2016 a jury convicted him, with a fellow former detective named Glen McNamara, of murdering a 20-year-old student, Jamie Gao, in a storage unit in the Sydney suburb of Padstow. Both men were sentenced to life. He lost every appeal and died in custody in January 2024.

Other killings and shootings in his career, among them shootings he carried out as a police officer and the deaths of people who accused him, were examined by inquests and trials, and the outcomes were more ambiguous. Those cases are set out below with the result each one produced.
content.h2: From Bankstown to the hold-up squad
content.p: The ABC and The Guardian give his birth year as 1941. The Guardian's profile says he was born in Paddington, the son of a Yorkshire boilermaker and a Welsh soprano, and grew up on an acre of land in Sydney's west, where he rode a mare to school. SBS says he was a talented pianist as a child, a skill he later used to entertain at his mother's aged care home and among fellow prisoners.

Most sources date his entry to the police to 1958, when he was 17. One law firm's summary says 1959. SBS says he rose quickly and he became an integral member of the armed hold-up squad. The ABC counted at least a dozen bravery awards in his early years, and a police appraisal quoted in a 2014 Sydney Morning Herald profile called him "a polished performer, extremely enthusiastic worker, outstanding detective".

The 1980 Peter Mitchell Award, the highest annual police honour, came for the arrest of an escaped armed robber, Gary Purdey. By then he had already shot dead at least two men. The ABC's obituary records that on 26 June 1976 he killed the bank robber Phillip Western in a shootout at Avoca Beach, and that in 1977 he shot another bank robber, known as "Butchy" Burns. The Guardian's writer, who knew him in later life, says Rogerson had shot three men in the line of duty by the time he won the award.
content.h2: Warren Lanfranchi and the accusation of murder
content.p: In 1981 Rogerson shot dead Warren Lanfranchi, a 22-year-old heroin dealer, at a meeting in Dangar Place, Chippendale. Rogerson said he fired in self-defence because Lanfranchi had drawn a pistol. The Sydney Crime Museum notes that the 18 police in the area all supported his account, and none has publicly questioned it.

Accounts of the inquest differ. The ABC says it found Rogerson was acting in the line of duty and in self-defence. SBS and the Sydney Crime Museum say the jury declined to find that he had acted in self-defence, though SBS adds that he was cleared of wrongdoing. He was never charged.

The reason for the meeting remains disputed. The Sydney Crime Museum describes one theory, which police denied: that Lanfranchi had robbed a heroin dealer under police protection and had once pointed a gun at an officer. Lanfranchi's girlfriend, Sallie-Anne Huckstepp, went public with an accusation that he had been killed in cold blood. On Rogerson's side, he told a Sydney Morning Herald reporter in 1982 that he regretted the shooting but believed he acted in good faith, and that Lanfranchi would have shot him. Asked about allegations of corruption and heroin dealing, he replied that they were "completely untrue".

Huckstepp was found drowned in a pond in Centennial Park in February 1986. The man charged with her murder, the criminal Arthur "Neddy" Smith, was acquitted at a trial in 1999, and no one has been convicted. Rogerson has not been charged with her death. A columnist writing in the Port Macquarie News after his death said she was killed "at the suspected order of Rogerson", but that is an opinion piece's suspicion, not a finding by any court.
content.h2: Neddy Smith and the shooting of Michael Drury
content.p: Smith, a heroin distributor and armed robber, was Rogerson's best-known associate. In the Sydney Crime Museum's account, Smith later claimed that Rogerson and colleagues gave him a "green light" to commit crime as a reward for delivering Lanfranchi to the meeting. The police deny that. The Crown prosecutor at Smith's 1999 trial told the jury the same thing about the green light, according to SBS. Rogerson told the ABC in 2006 that the relationship was only friendship, and that they were not "colluding or conspiring to commit crime".
Neddy Smith himself called the relationship one of convenience: "He used me to suit his own purposes."

In June 1984 the drug squad detective Michael Drury was shot twice through his kitchen window at home on Sydney's north shore. The ABC says he was feeding his three-year-old daughter. Drury, who survived, said Rogerson had tried to bribe him to change evidence in a heroin trial and that he had refused. Rogerson was charged with conspiring in the attempted murder and was acquitted in 1989. According to the Sydney Crime Museum, Flannery was later found to have been hired to kill Drury, and Rogerson had provided an alibi for him.

Independent Commission Against Corruption Commissioner Ian Temby wrote in 1994 that Rogerson's dealings with Smith "brought discredit on the Police Service, and must be described as scandalous", according to SBS.

Rogerson was dismissed from the police in 1986. He has said the cause was a misunderstanding about some gold coins and blamed the commissioner of the time, Jack Avery, for a campaign against him. The ABC and others link the dismissal to a bank-account matter, but the sources do not agree on the sequence, so it is safest to say only that he left the force in 1986 under a cloud.

The offence for which he first went to prison involved more than $100,000 deposited in accounts under false names. A Sydney Morning Herald report says it came to light because he was overheard telling his then wife, Joy, where the money was while a jury was out in the Drury trial. He was convicted of perverting the course of justice, and in the Herald's account he appealed successfully at first, but the appeal was quashed in 1992 and he was jailed at Berrima until 1995. The ABC says he served more than three years. In a later interview he said that, while in prison, two officials from the Wood Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service offered him release on a special licence in return for testimony about senior police, and that he tore the form up.

In February 2005 a judge sentenced him to two years for lying to the Police Integrity Commission in 1999, when he claimed he did not know that his friend Sam Masri, a Liverpool Council manager, was corrupt. He pleaded guilty. The ABC says he served 12 months in Kirkconnell Correctional Centre, and his wife Anne Melocco received two years' periodic detention for the same offence. The Herald's later profile reports that a psychiatrist told the court he showed signs of depression and cognitive decline, and that the prosecutor suggested it might be an act. Rogerson was paroled in February 2006.

Outside prison he turned his notoriety into work. He supplied scaffolding, appeared on stage with the standover man Mark "Chopper" Read and the footballer Mark Jackson in a comedy show, and in 2009 published an autobiography, The Dark Side. The 1995 television series Blue Murder, in which Richard Roxburgh played him, had already taken him to a wide audience, and he blamed the show for burying him "beneath the stories, jokes, lies, exaggerations and sheer entertainment".

Jamie Gao was a 20-year-old university student whom the sentencing judge described as involved in the drug trade. In early 2014 he began meeting McNamara, a former detective and private investigator who wrote true-crime books. The jury heard the two met at least 27 times and exchanged hundreds of texts. McNamara said it was research for a book on Asian crime gangs; prosecutors rejected that and said the contact was preparation for a killing.

At 1.46 p.m. on 20 May 2014 security cameras at the Padstow storage facility showed Gao entering unit 803 with McNamara. A little more than three minutes later Rogerson, hobbling, went in. According to the Herald and Sydney Criminal Lawyers, about half an hour later the two men were filmed dragging a silver surfboard bag. Gao had been shot twice in the chest. A fisherman found the body floating off Cronulla six days later, according to the Herald, though other reports say it was found on the Monday after the killing.

Police arrested McNamara on 26 May 2014. Rogerson was in Queensland on a speaking tour and was arrested at his Padstow home the next day. His lawyer complained that the arrest was staged for the cameras, and police said it was an operational decision.

At trial, each man said the other had done it. McNamara said Rogerson shot Gao, then threatened McNamara and his daughters to force him to help dispose of the body. Rogerson said he walked in on a "nightmare", found Gao dead, and was told Gao had shot himself in a struggle. He told the jury he had never met Gao. The Crown said the plan was to kill Gao and take the 2.78 kilograms of methamphetamine he had brought, and pointed to the purchase of a station wagon on 27 April, with a receipt found in McNamara's apartment bearing Rogerson's fingerprint. Two pillowcases of the drug were later found under the seat of that car.

Prosecutors did not have to prove which man fired, only that the two had agreed to kill or seriously injure Gao. After a trial that the Herald said ran for 18 weeks, the jury found both men guilty of murder and of stealing the drug.

On 2 September 2016 Justice Geoffrey Bellew sentenced both men to life. He said he could not decide beyond reasonable doubt which of them shot Gao but was satisfied that one of them had, and that Gao "was executed in cold blood, just as the offenders had planned". He described the enterprise as "extensive in its planning, brutal in its execution and callous in its aftermath". Gao's family called it the best outcome they could have hoped for, while objecting that Gao had in effect been found guilty of drug offences "in the court of public opinion" without any chance to answer.

In July 2021 a bench of the NSW Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed both men's challenges to their convictions. Justice Andrew Bell said the Crown had made out a circumstantial case, and that both men had run "cut-throat defences". In March 2023 the High Court refused Rogerson leave to appeal. His barrister had argued that being unable to cross-examine McNamara fully caused a miscarriage of justice. The Crown said its case depended mainly on CCTV footage and not on McNamara's evidence.

During another trial in 2017, that of the developer Ron Medich over a separate murder, a witness named Fortunato "Lucky" Gattellari said he had asked Rogerson, who visited him in prison in April 2014, to help carry a proposal to Medich in exchange for silence. Gattellari said police knew of the scheme and that he called Rogerson and McNamara "2 f---wits" in his diary. Medich was later convicted of the murder.

Rogerson died at Prince of Wales Hospital on 21 January 2024 after being moved from Long Bay's aged care unit, where he had been bedridden for seven months. At the inquest in October 2024 deputy state coroner Elizabeth Ryan found he died of an intracerebral haemorrhage and said he had received "timely and appropriate care". The Premier, Chris Minns, said only that Rogerson's life had been "a lifetime of, in many cases, dishonour to the NSW Police Force". Rogerson denied to the end that he had known of any plan to kill Gao.
